summary: Defines common requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs, which are large NATs run by internet providers to share addresses among many customers. It updates RFC 4787. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Sets the rules for the giant shared mailroom a whole town uses, so mail from different houses does not get mixed up.

subtitle: The minimum rules an ISP-run NAT must follow so that many customers can share one public IPv4 address fairly and with fewer broken apps.

tldr.problem: ISPs short of IPv4 addresses put many subscribers behind one shared public address using a Carrier-Grade NAT, and a badly behaved CGN can break applications or let one customer starve the others.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds 15 requirements on top of the existing NAT behavior documents: paired address pooling, per-subscriber port limits, a 120 second wait before reusing ports, subscriber control through PCP, and guidance on logging and port allocation.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 4787. It is explicitly not an endorsement of CGNs, only a minimal set of requirements to raise the chance that applications work across them.

today: RFC 6888 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 127) that updates RFC 4787. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why CGNs Need Common Rules
sections.content:
With IPv4 addresses running short, an ISP may give each subscriber a private address and let a Network Address Translator (NAT) in its own network translate to a shared public address. If the customer also has a NAT at home, the traffic goes through two layers of NAT. The RFC notes that some ISPs offered this kind of service long before addresses ran short, so shortage is not the only driver.

The document is careful about its own role. It is not an IETF endorsement of CGNs or a real specification for them. It is a minimal set of requirements meant to increase the likelihood of applications working across CGNs.

Because subscribers no longer have unique IPv4 addresses, CGNs bring substantial limitations. Some applications need substantial enhancements and some may not work at all; RFC 6269 covers those issues. The new requirements are added on top of the generic NAT documents RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508, which still apply.
sections.eli5: When too many houses share one street address, some things get confusing. These rules try to keep the confusion small.

sections.title: What a Carrier-Grade NAT Is
sections.content:
A Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) is a NAT-based logical function used to share the same IPv4 address among several subscribers, and it is not managed by the subscribers. The words "carrier-grade" say nothing about quality. They describe where the NAT sits: in the ISP's network, translating the traffic of potentially many subscribers, who have limited or no control over it.

The CGN in this document is IPv4-only, and IPv6 address translation is not considered. It can still appear in a setup with IPv6 parts: Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) uses an IPv4-only CGN function with IPv6 encapsulation, so the requirements also apply to the CGN part of DS-Lite.

The RFC describes two topologies. In the common one, an internal realm of customer premises equipment sits behind the CGN, which has an external address pool. In the other, a hotspot, there is no customer premises equipment and so no second NAT layer, but the CGN serves customers who do not trust each other. The requirements are driven by fairness and robustness, which apply in both cases.
sections.eli5: A CGN is a shared mailroom run by the town, not by any one family. The families cannot change its rules.

sections.title: Sharing Addresses and Ports Fairly
sections.content:
The core requirements decide how the shared resources are handed out.

  • REQ-1: a CGN that forwards a transport protocol MUST meet that protocol's NAT behavior document: RFC 4787 for UDP, RFC 5382 for TCP, RFC 5508 for ICMP and RFC 5597 for DCCP.
  • REQ-2: the default IP address pooling behavior MUST be Paired, so all sessions from one internal address, whether TCP, UDP, ICMP or a mix, use the same external address. An administrator MAY change this per application protocol.
  • REQ-3: the CGN SHOULD NOT limit the size or contiguity of the external pool, and MUST accept contiguous or non-contiguous ranges.
  • REQ-7: it is RECOMMENDED to use endpoint-independent filtering, because some games and peer-to-peer applications need it. Address-Dependent Filtering MAY be used if it is known not to break the application.

Two requirements protect subscribers from each other. REQ-4 says a CGN MUST support limiting the number of external ports (or ICMP identifiers) assigned per subscriber, and that the limits MUST be configurable by the administrator. It is also RECOMMENDED to have thresholds that stop one subscriber from using excessive CPU, for example by rate-limiting new mappings. REQ-5 says a CGN SHOULD be able to limit the state memory per mapping and per subscriber, and the rate at which that state is allocated.
sections.eli5: Each family gets a limited number of mailboxes so one greedy family cannot use them all. And a family keeps the same street address for all its mail, so friends can still find it.

sections.title: Pass-Through, Port Reuse and Failure Behavior
sections.content:
REQ-6 says it MUST be possible to administratively turn off translation for specific destination addresses or ports. This suits servers inside the ISP's own network that the internal realm can already reach by normal routing. The CGN can then forward packets unchanged like a plain router, which the RFC says may be an important efficiency gain.

REQ-8 says once an external port is freed, it SHOULD NOT be given to a new mapping until at least 120 seconds have passed. The value matches the Maximum Segment Lifetime from RFC 793. The aim is that old sessions break rather than get redirected to a different peer. The same wait applies to ports that were in use when the CGN lost state, for example after a crash or reboot. Exceptions allow immediate reuse when the CGN tracks TCP sessions, when ports are statically assigned and stay constant across state loss, or when the ports used address-dependent or address-and-port-dependent filtering. The wait time and the maximum number of ports in this state MUST be configurable.

REQ-9 says a CGN MUST implement a protocol that gives subscribers explicit control over NAT mappings, and that protocol SHOULD be the Port Control Protocol (RFC 6887). REQ-10 says CGN makers SHOULD make their equipment manageable.

REQ-11 covers what happens when a new mapping cannot be created because of resource limits or quotas. The CGN MUST drop the original packet, SHOULD send an ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 1 (Host Unreachable), SHOULD notify a management system, and MUST NOT delete existing mappings to make room. Code 1 is preferred over code 13 because it is a soft error, so TCP stacks do not abort the connection attempt.
sections.eli5: When a mailbox is freed, the mailroom waits a bit before giving it to someone new, so old letters do not land in the wrong house. If the mailroom is full, it turns away the new letter instead of throwing out mail already in progress.

sections.title: Logging for Abuse Handling
sections.content:
When many subscribers share an external address, a destination host sees only the translated address and port. To identify the subscriber behind an abuse report, the administrator may need to look up an external IPv4 address, port and timestamp. For that, the RFC lists what a CGN would need to log for each mapping: the transport protocol, a subscriber identifier, the external source address, the external source port and a timestamp. This list is informational and not a requirement.

A subscriber identifier uniquely identifies a subscriber. In a traditional NAT the internal source address is enough. In DS-Lite many subscribers share an internal address, so the identifier is the tunnel endpoint identifier, the B4's IPv6 address. The RFC admits the cost: a busy CGN may produce large logs that need a lot of storage.

REQ-12 says a CGN SHOULD NOT log destination addresses or ports unless required for administrative reasons, because destination logging creates privacy issues. It points to RFC 6302, whose logging recommendations for servers mean the CGN does not need to log destinations.
sections.eli5: The mailroom keeps a notebook of which family used which mailbox and when. It should not write down who the letters were sent to, because that is private.

sections.title: Port Allocation Trade-offs
sections.content:
A CGN's port allocation scheme faces three competing goals, each a SHOULD:

  • REQ-13: maximize port utilization, since external ports are a shared resource.
  • REQ-14: minimize log volume. Some schemes create one log entry per mapping, while others let many mappings share one compact entry.
  • REQ-15: make it hard for attackers to guess port numbers, because easily guessed ports expose subscribers to the attacks described in RFC 6056.

No scheme can be best at all three. A choice optimizes one at the expense of another, which is why these are soft requirements (SHOULD) rather than MUST.
sections.eli5: You want to use every mailbox, keep the notebook short and make mailbox numbers hard to guess. You usually cannot have all three at once, so you pick a balance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious subscriber who can spoof another subscriber's customer premises equipment may cause a denial of service to that subscriber by creating mappings up to the allowed limit. The RFC says an ISP can prevent this with ingress filtering as described in RFC 2827.

Because the document recommends endpoint-independent filtering as the default, it points to the security considerations of RFC 4787. NATs sometimes reassemble fragments, and a CGN would do so at presumably high data rates, so readers should be familiar with the issues in RFC 4963. The Deployment Considerations section adds only that CGNs bring several issues, covered in RFC 6269.
sections.eli5: A sneaky neighbor could pretend to be you and use up your mailboxes. The town can stop this by checking where letters really come from.

viz.caption: KEY CGN REQUIREMENTS AND THEIR STRENGTH (RFC 6888)

items.label: Paired pooling
items.desc: MUST be the default address pooling behavior.

items.label: Port limits
items.desc: MUST support per-subscriber limits on external ports.

items.label: State limits
items.desc: SHOULD limit state memory per mapping and per subscriber.

items.label: Pass-through
items.desc: MUST allow turning off translation for chosen destinations.

items.label: Port reuse
items.desc: SHOULD NOT reuse a freed port for at least 120 seconds.

items.label: Subscriber control
items.desc: MUST implement a mapping control protocol, SHOULD be PCP.

items.label: Quota exceeded
items.desc: MUST drop the packet and MUST NOT delete existing mappings.

items.label: Destination logging
items.desc: SHOULD NOT log destinations unless required.
